newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New NZ windmill raises energy, environmental hopes.
newsitem.headline: New NZ windmill raises energy, environmental hopes.

text.p: A New Zealand company has designed a windmill that it believes can produce electricity six to eight times more efficiently than conventional wind turbines, at about half the cost.
"Vortec 7", a wind turbine prototype nearing completion on a remote New Zealand hillside, could reduce the cost of environmentally friendly energy sources if tests pan out, industry specialists say.

Vortec Energy Ltd's turbine is assisted by an aerodynamic device called a diffuser, a shroud-shaped structure at the back of the turbine rotor. The diffuser is designed to create a low pressure region downstream, leading to a suction effect and doubling the windspeed at the rotor.

Paul van Lieshout, windpower engineering manager at Designpower, a division of state-owned power generator Electricity Corp of New Zealand, said there was no question that diffuser technology worked. It was just a matter of how well.
Designpower worked with Counties Power, the local energy company that will receive electricity generated from Vortec 7, in evaluating the turbine's potential impact on its network.
But some experts wonder if the turbine can translate impressive wind tunnel tests into reality?

"Those numbers seemed to stack up, the only problem was that it was a little bit unclear about the errors that might be included in them. That's really now what they (Vortec) have to try to figure out as well," van Lieshout told Reuters.
NEEDED SUITABLE CONSTRUCTION MATERIAL

Vortec was formed two years ago after reaching an agreement with U.S.-based aerospace contractor Northrop Grumman Corp, which developed the technology two decades ago. Under the deal, Vortec can use Northrop's turbine technology for 20 years.
Vortec managing director Robin Johannink said the problem with the technology two decades ago was that a suitable construction material could not be found.
Vortec thinks it has solved the problem by using a high tensile ferro cement.

Vortec 7 has a seven-metre (yard) blade and is expected to generate 1.1 to 1.2 megawatts, enough to supply 500-700 homes, Johannink told reporters at the windmill's site at Waikaretu, 100 km (60 miles) south of Auckland.
Comparable turbines in New Zealand have 45-metre blades and are rated at about half a megawatt.

Although Vortec 7 will stand 22 metres high, final production models will be taller at 55 metres with a 20- or 23-metre blade, supported by a single cylinder pipe and rated at a heftier 3.5 megawatts.
Johannink said he expects testing to last two years but that the company should have an idea about its viability later in April. The official launch is set for April 26.
The prototype will cost about NZ$5.0 million (US$3.44 million), and the full-sized production machine is estimated to cost between NZ$2.5 and NZ$3.0 million.

Vortec is an unlisted private company with 100 individual investors. It has 12 million shares on issue, which informally trade around NZ$2.00 each, and a prospectus is being prepared for a new issue of 2.0 million shares.
Despite New Zealand's strong winds, windpower has been slow to take off because the low cost of electricity generated from other sources such as hydro and gas.
WINDPOWER SEEN VALUABLE AS GAS FIELD NEARS DEPLETION
But energy analysts expect windpower to become more valuable when the nation's Maui gas field nears depletion mid-way through the next decade.
Meanwhile, public opposition to new hydroelectric projects remains an important political concern.
Vortec believes it can produce electricity at four NZ cents a kilowatt per hour compared to the present average cost of 4.5-5 cents from conventional sources.
"If that is the case, then that is very comparable with energy sources that we have operational right now," said van Lieshout. "If that is true then they have a winner."
Still the project has its critics, including Paul Gipe, a Bakersfield, California-based author and independent wind power analyst.
"It is extremely unlikely that this technology will offer any benefits over existing technology," he told Reuters.

"Time and time again, inventors have attempted to use diffuser technology to augment the power of the wind and invariably we've found that the diffuser technology adds additional expenses that offset any greater energy generation."
Gipe said it was much cheaper to simply extend the length of a conventional wind turbine rotor to gain more power.
"It is possible...that this company has some new technology that could be of use, but it is remote," he said.
